--- title: "Hands-on Exercise 7" subtitle: "Modelling Geographical Accessibility" author: "An Loc" date: "13 October 2026" date-modified: "last-modified" date-format: "D MMM YYYY" format: html: toc: true toc-depth: 4 toc-expand: true code-fold: false code-copy: true fig-width: 9 fig-height: 7 execute: echo: true eval: true warning: false message: false freeze: true --- # Overview In Exercise 6, townships were grouped into regions by the similarity of their ICT rates. In this exercise, accessibility is measured for every part of Singapore: how easily the residents of each part can reach one of the 120 eldercare centres in the government's list of eldercare services. On slide 3, accessibility is "the measure of the capacity of a location to be reached from, or to be reached by, different locations", the definition of Rodrigue et al. (2013). Every measure in this exercise combines demand, supply and the cost of travel: - the demand at each place, the number of people who may use the service; - the supply at each service location, the amount of service available; - the cost of travel between each place and each service location, here the network distance along the roads. **Part 1** is a reproduction of r4gdsa chapter 17, which computes three measures with the `ac()` function of the `SpatialAcc` package: Hansen's potential model, the kernel density two-step floating catchment area method (KD2SFCA) and the spatial accessibility measure (SAM). In **Part 2**, the output of `ac()` is compared with the formulas on the Lesson 7 slides and in the readings, and the distance matrix is checked. The 2SFCA and E2SFCA methods of slides 24 to 28 are added, and the constant demand of the chapter is replaced with the number of residents aged 65 and over. ::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"} ## Sources The hands-on exercise for Lesson 7 is this chapter: - [Chapter 17: Modelling Geographical Accessibility](https://r4gdsa.netlify.app/chap17.html) The Lesson 7 outline lists four readings for before the lesson. | Reading | What it contributes | Used in | |--------------------------|--------------------------------------------------------|----------------------| | **Long (2017)**, "Modelling Accessibility", GIS&T Body of Knowledge | Network space and network distance; four classes of accessibility measure; the remark that gravity-based measures have no clear definition of a high or low value, so "all analysis must be relative"; aggregation of accessibility to regions | 3.1, 4.1, 4.6 | | **Hansen (1959)**, *Accessibility and Residential Growth* | Accessibility as the sum of the opportunities at each zone divided by the separation raised to an exponent, and exponents of 2.2 to 3.0 by trip purpose | 3.1, 3.3, 3.4, 4.2, 4.3 | | **Luo and Wang (2003)**, "Measures of spatial accessibility to health care in a GIS environment" | The two steps of 2SFCA; 2SFCA as a special case of the gravity model with competition; the population-weighted mean of the accessibility scores equals the ratio of total supply to total demand; a larger catchment gives smoother scores | 3.1, 3.2, 3.4, 4.2 to 4.6 | | **Luo and Qi (2009)**, "An enhanced two-step floating catchment area (E2SFCA) method" | Three travel zones within the catchment, with weights from a Gaussian function | 4.2 to 4.6 | The outline links Hansen (1959) to a PDF at MIT. The PDF is Hansen's master's thesis of 1959, which contains the accessibility model and the exponents used on this page. Packages The chapter's code loads `ggstatsplot` and `reshape2`, but the two packages are not used, so they are left out on this page. `patchwork` is added to place maps side by side, and `knitr` to format tables. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} pacman::p_load(sf, SpatialAcc, tmap, patchwork, knitr, tidyverse) ``` ::: ::: {.callout-note collapse="false" title="How the code works"} ```r pacman::p_load(...) # pacman ``` - `p_load()` loads each package, and installs any that are missing. | Package | Used for | |------------------|----------------------------------------------------------------------------------| | `sf` | reading the shapefiles, coordinate reference systems, spatial joins | | `SpatialAcc` | `ac()`, the accessibility measures | | `tmap` | maps | | `patchwork` | placing several charts or maps in one figure | | `knitr` | tables | | `tidyverse` | reading and reshaping the distance matrix (`readr`, `dplyr`, `tidyr`), and `ggplot2` charts | ::: ## The data Section 17.2 of the chapter lists four data sets, which are distributed with the exercise on eLearn. | Data set | Format | Features | Contents | |-------------------------|--------------|------------------|-------------------------------------------| | `MP14_SUBZONE_NO_SEA_PL` | ESRI shapefile | 323 polygons | URA Master Plan 2014 subzone boundaries, from data.gov.sg | | `hexagons` | ESRI shapefile | 3,125 polygons | hexagons covering the main island, Jurong Island and Sentosa, made with `st_make_grid()` | | `ELDERCARE` | ESRI shapefile | 120 points | eldercare services, from data.gov.sg | | `OD_Matrix` | CSV | 375,000 rows, 6 fields | network distance in metres from every hexagon to every centre | According to the chapter, `hexagons`, `ELDERCARE` and `OD_Matrix` were prepared by Prof. Kam Tin Seong for teaching and research, and may be used for this hands-on exercise. Use of the three data sets for any other purpose requires the approval of Prof. Kam. ## Geospatial data ### Reading the three layers The three layers have separate roles in the computation of Part 1: | Object | Layer | One feature is | Used for | |----------|----------------------|------------------------|--------------------------------------------| | `hexagons` | `hexagons` | a hexagon of the main island, Jurong Island or Sentosa | demand in `ac()` (section 2.3.3) and rows of the distance matrix (section 2.4); unit of the Hansen, KD2SFCA and SAM scores (sections 3.1 to 3.3) | | `eldercare` | `ELDERCARE` | an eldercare service, with its postal code and address | supply in `ac()` (section 2.3.3) and columns of the distance matrix (section 2.4); red points on the maps of sections 3.1.2, 3.2.2 and 3.3.2 | | `mpsz` | `MP14_SUBZONE_NO_SEA_PL` | a subzone of the URA Master Plan 2014, with its planning area and region | region of each hexagon, for the boxplots of sections 3.1.3, 3.2.3 and 3.3.3 | ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} mpsz <- st_read(dsn = "data/geospatial", layer = "MP14_SUBZONE_NO_SEA_PL") hexagons <- st_read(dsn = "data/geospatial", layer = "hexagons") eldercare <- st_read(dsn = "data/geospatial", layer = "ELDERCARE") ``` ::: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} tibble(layer = c("mpsz", "hexagons", "eldercare"), features = c(nrow(mpsz), nrow(hexagons), nrow(eldercare)), geometry = c(as.character(st_geometry_type(mpsz, by_geometry = FALSE)), as.character(st_geometry_type(hexagons, by_geometry = FALSE)), as.character(st_geometry_type(eldercare, by_geometry = FALSE))), epsg = c(st_crs(mpsz)$epsg, st_crs(hexagons)$epsg, st_crs(eldercare)$epsg)) |> kable() ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} |layer | features|geometry | epsg| |:---------|--------:|:------------|----:| |mpsz | 323|MULTIPOLYGON | NA| |hexagons | 3125|POLYGON | 3414| |eldercare | 120|POINT | 3414| ::: ::: ::: {.callout-note collapse="false" title="How the code works"} ```r st_read(dsn, layer) # sf st_geometry_type(x, by_geometry = FALSE) # sf st_crs(x)$epsg # sf tibble(...) # tibble kable(x, digits) # knitr ``` - `st_read()` reads the shapefile named by `layer` from the folder `dsn` into a simple feature data frame. `results: hide` suppresses the report that `st_read()` prints for each file. - `st_geometry_type(by_geometry = FALSE)` returns one geometry type for the whole layer. - `st_crs()$epsg` returns the EPSG code of the coordinate reference system, or `NA` when the file does not contain one. - `tibble()` builds a data frame from vectors of equal length, one column for each argument. Here the table has one row for each layer. - `kable()` prints a data frame as a formatted table. The other tables on this page are also printed with `kable()`. Where `digits` is given, it rounds the numbers. ::: The subzones have no EPSG code: their projection file describes SVY21 by its parameters only. The hexagons and the eldercare centres are already in SVY21 with EPSG code 3414. The map below shows the hexagons, the subzone boundaries and the eldercare centres together. ::: {.panel-tabset} #### Map ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](Hands-on_Ex07_files/figure-html/layers-map-1.png){width=864} ::: ::: #### Code ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} tm_shape(hexagons) + tm_polygons(fill = "grey85", col = "white", lwd = 0.3) + tm_shape(mpsz) + tm_borders(col = "steelblue", lwd = 0.7) + tm_shape(eldercare) + tm_dots(fill = "red", size = 0.3) + tm_add_legend(type = "polygons", labels = "hexagons", fill = "grey85", col = "white") + tm_add_legend(type = "lines", labels = "subzone boundaries", col = "steelblue") + tm_add_legend(type = "symbols", labels = "eldercare centres", fill = "red") + tm_title("Hexagons, subzones and eldercare centres") + tm_layout(frame = FALSE, legend.outside = TRUE, legend.outside.position = "bottom") ``` ::: ::: {.callout-note collapse="false" title="How the code works"} ```r tm_shape(shp) + tm_polygons(fill, col, lwd) # tmap tm_borders(col, lwd) # tmap tm_dots(fill, size) # tmap tm_add_legend(type, labels, fill, col) # tmap ``` - Each `tm_shape()` starts a layer, and the layers are drawn in order: the hexagons in grey with white borders, the subzone boundaries in blue, and the centres as red points. - The extent and the coordinate reference system of the map are those of the first layer, `hexagons`. The subzones are in the same SVY21 projection as the hexagons, so the two layers line up although the EPSG code of the subzones is added only in section 2.3.2. - Each layer is drawn in one colour, so the legend is built by hand. `tm_add_legend()` adds one entry for each layer. ::: ::: Five subzones have no hexagon: the North-Eastern Islands (Pulau Ubin and Pulau Tekong), Pulau Seletar, Sudong, Semakau and the Southern Group. Of the 120 centres, 61 are in the Central Region, which has 136 km² of the 781 km² of land in the subzone layer. The West Region, with 257 km², has 20 centres. ### Coordinate reference system ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} mpsz <- st_transform(mpsz, 3414) eldercare <- st_transform(eldercare, 3414) hexagons <- st_transform(hexagons, 3414) st_crs(mpsz)$epsg ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 3414 ``` ::: ::: ::: {.callout-note collapse="false" title="How the code works"} ```r st_transform(x, crs) # sf ``` - `st_transform()` converts the coordinates of `x` to the coordinate reference system `crs`, here EPSG:3414, SVY21 / Singapore TM. For `hexagons` and `eldercare`, which are already in EPSG:3414, the call changes nothing. For `mpsz`, the call keeps the SVY21 projection and adds the EPSG code. ::: The chapter text names the subzone layer `MP14_SUBZONE_WEB_PL` and the transformed object `mpsz_svy21`. The chapter's code reads the layer `MP14_SUBZONE_NO_SEA_PL` into the object `mpsz`. ::: {.callout-tip collapse="false"} ## Hexagons as the spatial unit On slides 9 to 11, hexagons are the spatial unit. Administrative units such as subzones have shapes and sizes set by planning decisions. Every hexagon has the same area. Of the regular polygons that tile a plane, the hexagon is the closest to a circle. ::: {.cell} ::: Each hexagon covers 216,506 m². Its sides are 288.7 m long, and the distance from its centre to the middle of each side is 250 m. The "250m radius" of section 17.2 is that distance. The centres of two neighbouring hexagons are 500 m apart. ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](Hands-on_Ex07_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-7-1.png){width=864} ::: ::: The hexagons are the units of demand in every measure on this page. The demand of a hexagon is placed at its centre point. The distance to each eldercare centre is measured from that point. ::: ### Demand and capacity The layers read in section 2.3.1 have no field for the demand of a hexagon or the capacity of a centre. The code below adds a `demand` column to `hexagons` and a `capacity` column to `eldercare`. It also keeps only the identifier `fid` of `hexagons` and `eldercare`, and the postal code of each centre. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} eldercare <- eldercare |> select(fid, ADDRESSPOS) |> mutate(capacity = 100) hexagons <- hexagons |> select(fid) |> mutate(demand = 100) ``` ::: ::: {.callout-note collapse="false" title="How the code works"} ```r select(.data, ...) # dplyr mutate(.data, ...) # dplyr ``` - `select()` keeps the identifier `fid` of each layer, and the postal code of each centre. The geometry column is kept by `sf` without being named. - `mutate()` adds a constant column to each layer: a capacity of 100 for each centre, and a demand of 100 for each hexagon. `eldercare` has 20 columns when it is read. With the default `skip = 0`, reading starts at the first line. - `glimpse()` prints the number of rows and columns, and the type and first values of each column. ::: The file has one row per pair of hexagon and eldercare centre: 3,125 hexagons × 120 centres = 375,000 rows. ::: {.callout-tip collapse="false"} ## Fields of the distance matrix Each row gives the cost of travel, in metres, from the centre of one hexagon to one eldercare centre, divided into these parts: | Field | Distance | |--------------------|--------------------------------------------------------------------------------| | `entry_cost` | from the centre of the hexagon to the nearest road | | `network_cost` | along the road network | | `exit_cost` | from the road to the eldercare centre | | `total_cost` | the sum of `entry_cost`, `network_cost` and `exit_cost` | The invented street map below draws the `entry_cost`, `network_cost` and `exit_cost` of one pair of hexagon and centre as three coloured lines. ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](Hands-on_Ex07_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-10-1.png){width=864} ::: ::: The table shows the first three rows of the file, which give the distances from hexagon 1 to the first three centres. ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output-display} | origin_id| destination_id| entry_cost| network_cost| exit_cost| total_cost| |---------:|--------------:|----------:|------------:|---------:|----------:| | 1| 1| 667.9| 19846.9| 47.6| 20562.5| | 1| 2| 667.9| 45026.8| 31.9| 45726.6| | 1| 3| 667.9| 17644.2| 173.5| 18485.6| ::: ::: Kalogirou and Foley (2006), the source of SAM, computed their distances in the same three parts: from the centroid of each district to the nearest node of the road network, along the network, and from the network to the hospital. Long (2017, section 2.2) gives the reason for distances along the network: "most human movement occurs along a spatial network consisting of roads, railways, and paths". Slide 6 shows the straight-line ("Cartesian") distance and the network distance of the same trip. ::: ### From long to wide `ODMatrix` has one row for each pair of hexagon and eldercare centre. `ac()` takes a matrix with one row for each hexagon and one column for each centre. `identical()` compares two vectors position by position, and returns `TRUE` only when every position holds the same value. The table shows the first positions of the column names of `distmat` and of `eldercare$fid`. | | 1st | 2nd | 3rd | 4th | 5th | 6th | 7th | … | |------------------------------------|------|------|------|------|------|------|------|------| | column names of `distmat` | 1 | 2 | 3 | 4 | 5 | 6 | 8 | … | | `eldercare$fid` | 1 | 2 | 3 | 4 | 5 | 6 | 8 | … | | the same names sorted as text | 1 | **10** | **100** | **101** | **103** | **104** | **105** | … | The column names of `distmat` and `eldercare$fid` are the same at every position, so `identical()` returns `TRUE`. Then `ac()` would pair the second column, centre 10, with the capacity of centre 2. ::: `ac()` matches the matrix to the demand and the capacity by position: row $i$ to the $i$-th hexagon, column $j$ to the $j$-th centre. The chapter's code includes no check of the order. The row check and the column check return `TRUE`, so the rows of `distmat` follow the order of `hexagons` and the columns follow the order of `eldercare`. The 120 centres have identifiers between 1 and 133, with gaps. The columns of `distmat` follow the order of the identifiers. After the first gap, the `fid` of the $j$-th centre is larger than $j$. The Hansen, KD2SFCA and SAM measures are each computed with `ac()`, joined to the hexagons, mapped, and compared across the five regions of the Master Plan. ## Hansen's potential model ::: {.callout-tip collapse="false"} ## The potential model of Hansen (1959) Hansen (1959) defines accessibility as "the potential of opportunities for interaction". The definition comes from Stewart's potential of population (slide 19). Hansen describes that potential as "directly proportional to the size of the group (activity level) and inversely proportional to the distance or separation from that group". In Hansen's formula, the accessibility of zone $i$ is a sum over all zones $j$. In this exercise, zone $i$ is a hexagon and zone $j$ is an eldercare centre: $$A_i = \sum_j \frac{S_j}{T_{ij}^{\,x}} = \sum_j \frac{\text{capacity of centre } j}{(\text{road distance from hexagon } i \text{ to centre } j)^{x}}$$ $x$ is an exponent of distance. The contribution of a centre to the score of a hexagon increases with the capacity of the centre and decreases with the distance between the centre and the hexagon. A larger $x$ makes the contribution decrease faster with distance. In the speaker notes of slide 7, the power function is traced to Newton's law of gravitation, the origin of the term gravity model. According to the same notes, $x$ is large for grocery shopping, because people travel only a short distance for groceries. For furniture shopping, $x$ is small, because people travel farther than for groceries. The formula has no catchment, so every centre adds to the score of every hexagon, at any distance. The example below has one hexagon and three centres, with $x = 2$. The distances and capacities are invented for this example. A line joins the hexagon to each centre. A wider line marks a larger term $S_j/T_{ij}^2$. ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](Hands-on_Ex07_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-15-1.png){width=864} ::: ::: Centre B is twice as far from the hexagon as centre A, so its term is a quarter of the term of centre A. Centre C is as far from the hexagon as centre B and has four times the capacity of centre B, so the term of centre C is four times the term of centre B, the same as the term of centre A. Slide 8 shows two forms of distance decay: the power function $\alpha / d^{\beta}$ and the exponential function $\alpha e^{-\beta d}$. Hansen (1959, p. 5) uses the power function, which is $1/d^2$ with $x = 2$. The `SpatialAcc` manual describes `power` as "the power of the separation variable". The source of `ac()`, printed in section 4.2, computes the exponential function: with `power = 2`, the value in the chapter's code, the weight is $e^{-2d}$, where $d$ is the road distance in kilometres. The table compares the weights of $1/d^2$ and $e^{-2d}$, each relative to the weight of a centre 1 km away: | Function | Formula | 1 km | 2 km | 4 km | 8 km | Rule | |----------------------|----------|------------|------------|------------|------------------|----------------------------------------| | Hansen (1959), $x = 2$ | $1/d^2$ | 1 | $1/4$ | $1/16$ | $1/64$ | divided by 4 each time the distance doubles | | `ac()`, `power = 2` | $e^{-2d}$ | 1 | $1/7$ | $1/403$ | $1/1{,}202{,}604$ | divided by $e^2 = 7.4$ for each extra kilometre | The weight of the power function depends on the ratio of two distances, and the weight of the exponential function on their difference. ::: ### Hansen scores from `ac()` The distance matrix holds 375,000 road distances, one for each pair of hexagon and centre. On slide 24, 2SFCA is described as "a special case of a potential model". The table explains the three terms in the name 2SFCA: | Term | Meaning | |----------------|--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------| | catchment | the area within a threshold distance $d_0$ of a point, here 5 km by road | | floating | a catchment of the same size, drawn around one point after another | | two-step | a catchment drawn twice: around every centre in step 1, then around every hexagon in step 2 | In Luo and Wang (2003), the circle "floats from one centroid to another while its radius remains the same". They trace 2SFCA to an earlier floating catchment area method with one step. That method draws a circle around each residential location. The accessibility of the location is the ratio of physicians to residents inside the circle, as if those physicians served only those residents. Luo and Wang (2003) call this assumption "obviously faulty": a physician inside the circle also serves residents outside it. Slides 25 and 26 show the two steps of 2SFCA, with physicians as the supply and residents as the demand. In this exercise, the supply is the capacity of a centre and the demand is the population of a hexagon: 1. **Step 1, from each centre.** The ratio $R_j$ is the capacity of centre $j$ divided by the demand of all hexagons within $d_0$ of the centre. $R_j$ is the capacity per person in the catchment of the centre. When more people live in the catchment, $R_j$ is smaller. 2. **Step 2, from each hexagon.** The accessibility $A_i$ of hexagon $i$ is the sum of $R_j$ over all centres within $d_0$ of the hexagon. In the chapter, the chunk is described as calculating "Hansen's accessibility", a description copied from section 17.6, which covers the Hansen measure. ::: ::: {.callout-tip collapse="false"} ## The 2SFCA formula and an example Luo and Wang (2003, equations 3 and 4) write the two steps as $$R_j = \frac{S_j}{\sum_{k:\, d_{kj} \le d_0} P_k} = \frac{\text{capacity of centre } j}{\text{demand of the hexagons within } d_0 \text{ of centre } j}$$ $$A_i = \sum_{j:\, d_{ij} \le d_0} R_j = \text{sum of } R_j \text{ over the centres within } d_0 \text{ of hexagon } i$$ where $S_j$ is the capacity of centre $j$ and $P_k$ is the demand of hexagon $k$. In an invented example of four hexagons and two centres, centre A has a capacity of 1, centre B has a capacity of 3, and the catchment is 5 km: ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output-display} | | km to A| km to B| demand|centres within 5 km | by hand| ac(family = "2SFCA")| |:---------|-------:|-------:|------:|:-------------------|-------:|--------------------:| |hexagon 1 | 1| 6| 100|A | 0.0025| 0.0025| |hexagon 2 | 2| 4| 200|A, B | 0.0100| 0.0100| |hexagon 3 | 4| 2| 100|A, B | 0.0100| 0.0100| |hexagon 4 | 6| 1| 100|B | 0.0075| 0.0075| ::: ::: The scores from `ac()` are the same as the hand calculation for all four hexagons. **Unit.** The scores have a unit: capacity per person. **Average.** Luo and Wang (2003) show that the average of the scores, weighted by demand, equals the total capacity divided by the total demand. In the example, $(100 \times 0.0025 + 200 \times 0.01 + 100 \times 0.01 + 100 \times 0.0075) / 500 = 0.008 = 4 / 500$. The same check is applied to the eldercare data in section 4.4. ::: ::: {.callout-tip collapse="false"} ## The KD2SFCA formula in `ac()` In KD2SFCA, step 1 and step 2 of 2SFCA are each weighted by a kernel that falls with distance. According to the source of `ac()` (section 4.2), the kernel is $e^{-d^{\beta}}$, where $\beta$ is `power`: $$R_j = \frac{n_j}{\sum_{k:\, d_{kj} \le d_0} p_k \, e^{-d_{kj}^{\beta}}}, \qquad A_i = \sum_{j:\, d_{ij} \le d_0} R_j \, e^{-d_{ij}^{\beta}}$$ With `power = 2` and `d0 = 5`, a hexagon or centre inside the 5 km catchment has the weight $e^{-d^2}$, with $d$ in kilometres. A hexagon or centre outside the catchment has the weight 0. A larger $\beta$ gives a larger weight below 1 km and a smaller weight above it, and every weight is 0 beyond 5 km (chart below; the dashed line is 2SFCA, with a weight of 1 inside the catchment). ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output-display} ```{=html}

Kalogirou and Foley (2006) describe SAM as "a population-weighted accessibility score". According to them, accessibility "increased the greater the local population and the number and/or size of facilities in the system" and "decreased the greater the distances from the place in question to those facilities". The source of `ac()`, about 50 lines long, is printed by typing the name of the function: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} SpatialAcc::ac ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` function (p, n, D, d0, power = 2, family = "SAM") { family <- match.arg(family, c("SAM", "2SFCA", "KD2SFCA", "Hansen", "log")) D <- as.matrix(D) if (length(p) != nrow(D)) { stop("length of 'p' must equal nrow(D)") } if (length(n) != ncol(D)) { stop("length of 'n' must equal ncol(D)") } if (family %in% c("2SFCA", "KD2SFCA") && missing(d0)) { stop("'d0' is required for family '2SFCA' and 'KD2SFCA'") } if (family == "SAM") { ac.matrix <- t(n/t(p * (D^power))) ac.measure <- rowSums(ac.matrix) } else if (family == "2SFCA") { D[D > d0] <- 0 D[D > 0] <- 1 step1 <- p * D Rj <- n/colSums(step1) step2 <- t(Rj * t(D)) step2[is.nan(step2)] <- 0 ac.measure <- rowSums(step2) } else if (family == "KD2SFCA") { D[D > d0] <- 0 D0 <- D D0[D > 0] <- 1 step1 <- p * exp(-D^power) step1 <- step1 * D0 Rj <- n/colSums(step1) step2 <- t(Rj * t(exp(-D^power))) step2 <- step2 * D0 step2[is.nan(step2)] <- 0 ac.measure <- rowSums(step2) } else if (family == "Hansen") { ac.matrix <- n * exp(-power * D) ac.measure <- rowSums(ac.matrix) } else { ac.matrix <- log(n * exp(-power * D))/power ac.measure <- rowSums(ac.matrix) } return(ac.measure) } ``` ::: ::: The table lists each value of the `family` argument of `ac()` beside its definition in the slides and the readings. | Family | Computed by `ac()` | In the slides or the readings | Difference | |-----------|---------------------------|-------------------------------------|-------------------------| | `Hansen` | $\sum_j n_j e^{-\beta d_{ij}}$ | Hansen (1959, p. 5): $\sum_j S_j / T_{ij}^{x}$; The kernel gives weights below 0.018 beyond 2 km (section 4.2). In 2SFCA (slides 24 to 26), every centre within the catchment counts equally. In E2SFCA (slides 27 and 28), the catchment is divided into three zones with decreasing weights. In KD2SFCA (Polzin et al., 2014), a continuous kernel replaces the zones. Luo and Wang (2003) computed 2SFCA with seven catchments, from 20 to 50 minutes, and found that the scores had a lower variance with a larger catchment. Luo and Qi (2009) computed E2SFCA with two sets of zone weights. On p. 1104, they report that 2SFCA gives higher scores than E2SFCA in areas of poor access, which they attribute to the assumption of equal access inside the catchment in 2SFCA. They also find that 2SFCA identifies a smaller total shortage area than E2SFCA. With the weights of set 2, which decrease faster with distance, E2SFCA identifies a larger total shortage area than with the weights of set 1 (Luo and Qi, 2009, p. 1104; speaker notes of slide 28). Polzin et al. (2014) compared the Epanechnikov kernel of Dai and Wang (2011) with a quartic kernel. Cheng et al. (2016) set the width of a Gaussian kernel so that the weight at the edge of the catchment is 0.05. Luo and Wang (2003) show that, in 2SFCA, the average accessibility weighted by demand equals the total supply divided by the total demand, provided every centre has some demand within its catchment. The capacity of each centre is allocated to the hexagons in its catchment. In E2SFCA and KD2SFCA, the same weights enter step 1 and step 2, so the capacity is allocated in the same way, and the same equality holds. The question for this section is how much the scores depend on the kernel and on the size of the catchment, and whether each computation satisfies the property of Luo and Wang (2003). ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} fca_weights <- function(D, kernel, d0 = 5) { W <- switch(kernel, step = (D <= d0) * 1, ac_default = exp(-D^2) * (D <= d0), epanechnikov = (1 - (D / d0)^2) * (D <= d0), cheng = exp(-D^2 / (d0^2 / log(20))) * (D <= d0), e2sfca_1 = c(1, 0.68, 0.22, 0)[findInterval(D, c(d0 / 3, 2 * d0 / 3, d0), left.open = TRUE) + 1], e2sfca_2 = c(1, 0.42, 0.09, 0)[findInterval(D, c(d0 / 3, 2 * d0 / 3, d0), left.open = TRUE) + 1]) matrix(W, nrow = nrow(D)) } fca <- function(p, n, D, kernel, d0 = 5) { W <- fca_weights(D, kernel, d0) R <- n / colSums(p * W) R[!is.finite(R)] <- 0 as.vector(W %*% R) } ``` ::: ::: {.callout-note collapse="false" title="How the code works"} - `fca_weights()` returns a matrix of the same shape as `D`, with the weight of each pair under one kernel. `(D <= d0)` is `TRUE` inside the catchment and `FALSE` outside, which become 1 and 0 when multiplied. For E2SFCA, `findInterval()` returns 0, 1, 2 or 3 for a distance in the first, second or third zone or beyond the catchment. The weight is then looked up in a vector of four zone weights. The zones are thirds of the catchment, in place of the 10-minute zones of a 30-minute catchment on slide 27. The zone weights of `e2sfca_1` and `e2sfca_2` are weight sets 1 and 2 of Luo and Qi (2009). - `fca()` computes the two steps of section 3.2.1 with any kernel. `colSums(p * W)` is the weighted demand in the catchment of each centre (`p * W` multiplies row $i$ of `W` by the demand of hexagon $i$), and `R` is the ratio of capacity to weighted demand for each centre. According to the chapter, the actual demand should be used in practice. Kalogirou and Foley (2006) measured the demand for hospitals by the population aged 65 and over, as "the population sub-group who would be most likely to be the heaviest users". Luo and Wang (2003) and Luo and Qi (2009) took the demand from census counts of the population. Polzin et al. In this exercise, the demand for eldercare is measured by the residents aged 65 and over, as in Kalogirou and Foley (2006). Exercise 1 used the 2020 census table of residents by subzone, age and sex from SingStat. The census counts residents by subzone, and the measures require a count for each hexagon. Areal weighting divides the count of each subzone among the hexagons in proportion to the area of the subzone that each hexagon covers. The method assumes that the residents are spread evenly over each subzone. The three maps of Part 1 show the same pattern: high scores in the city centre and around each eldercare centre, and low scores in the west, the reservoir areas and the far east. In Part 2, I found that the scores depend on the distance matrix, the formula inside `ac()`, the size of the catchment and the demand. **The distance matrix has errors.** 159 hexagons have one distance to all 120 centres, the distance to the last centre in the file. One of them is within 5 km of every centre in the matrix. Under 2SFCA, it was the highest-scoring hexagon until I removed the 159 hexagons. The other 158 hexagons score 0 under KD2SFCA in Part 1. Of the 159 hexagons, 94 hexagons have a centre within 5 km in a straight line, so their scores of 0 come from wrong distances. I found the errors by comparing the network distances with straight-line distances. Some valid distances are also much longer than the straight line: centre 370093 is 125 m from hexagon 2479 in a straight line and 5.6 km away by road. With a catchment of 2 or 3 km, its capacity is lost. **Three measures of `ac()` differ from the formulas on the slides and in the readings.** Its Hansen measure uses an exponential decay, where Hansen (1959) used a power of distance. When the capacities of the centres differ, the Hansen measure also multiplies the weights of one centre by the capacity of another centre. Its KD2SFCA kernel has no width. With distances in kilometres, the weights beyond 2 km are below 0.02, so a catchment of 5 km has the effect of a catchment of about 2 km. The KD2SFCA scores also change with the unit of distance. Its SAM does not use `d0`. It uses the demand once, where the formula on slide 29 uses it twice. With a constant demand, its SAM equals a Hansen measure with the power function $1/d^2$, divided by the demand. None of these differences appears in the chapter's output. I found each difference by reading the source of `ac()`, which is about 50 lines long. **The floating catchment scores are a capacity per person.** The unit is the same for 2SFCA, E2SFCA and KD2SFCA. The mean of their scores weighted by demand equals the national ratio, a property derived by Luo and Wang (2003). Every computation of these methods with a catchment of 5 km or more satisfies the property. With a catchment of 2 or 3 km, one centre has no hexagon within its catchment, and the mean falls below the ratio. The Hansen and SAM scores have no unit. They can be compared only as ranks or ratios between hexagons, as Long (2017) says of gravity-based measures. **The demand changes the ratios of the centres more than the scores of the hexagons.** With the residents aged 65 and over in place of a constant demand of 100, the rank correlation is 0.98 for the hexagon scores and 0.64 for the centre ratios. **Regions under the census demand.** With the KD2SFCA kernel of Cheng et al. (2016), the score of every region outside the Central Region is below the national ratio. The North-East Region has the lowest score. In the North Region, 6.5% of the residents aged 65 and over have no centre within 5 km by road, the largest share of the five regions. **Limits.** Every centre has a capacity of 100, because the data have no measure of the size of a centre. Areal weighting spreads the residents of a subzone evenly over its area, including its parks and industrial land. The census is from 2020. The records of the centres were last updated in July 2016, according to the field `FMEL_UPD_D` of the shapefile. The chapter gives no information on the road network used for `OD_Matrix.csv`.
